topics: 🔗 A Prohibition Landing on a Prohibition — Rabbi Meir's exceptions: inclusive and expanded prohibitions still take effect
🍽️ Building the Five Liabilities — how chelev, impurity, hekdesh, notar, and Yom Kippur stack on one bite
❓ Why Not Five, Six, or Even More? — the Gemara tests and rejects several ways to expand the mishna's count
👨‍👩‍👧 One Act, Six or Seven Sins — an escalating series of mishnayot on forbidden relations that compound
⚖️ Rabbi Yosei's Added Case — reconciling his father's-wife addition with his own view on competing prohibitions

overview.title: 📖 Overview: How Prohibitions Stack on One Another
overview.subtitle: Keritot 14a–14b
overview.label: The scene:
overview.text: The daf opens with a foundational question: does a new prohibition take legal effect on an item already forbidden by an earlier prohibition? Rabbi Meir generally says no — except when the new prohibition is either 'inclusive' (issur kolel, extending the forbidden scope to new people or contexts) or 'expanded' (issur mosif, adding a new dimension of severity). Using this distinction, the Gemara explains exactly how the previous daf's case of one bite generating four sin offerings and one guilt offering actually works, then fends off several attempts to push the count even higher. The daf then pivots to a series of escalating mishnayot: one act of forbidden intercourse that violates six, then seven, forbidden-relation prohibitions simultaneously, built through the same logic of expanding and inclusive prohibitions layering onto a single relationship.

slides.title: 🔗 A Prohibition Landing on a Prohibition
slides.subtitle: Rabbi Meir's general rule, and its two exceptions
slides.hebrewSource: נְהִי דְּאִיסּוּר חָל עַל אִיסּוּר לֵית לֵיהּ, אִיסּוּר כּוֹלֵל וְאִיסּוּר מוֹסִיף אִית לֵיהּ
slides.label: The principle:
slides.text: Rabbi Meir holds that, as a rule, a second prohibition cannot take effect on an object or person already forbidden by an earlier one — the first prohibition already covers the case, so nothing new is added. But he recognizes two exceptions. An inclusive prohibition (issur kolel) does take effect, because it extends the forbidden scope to new people or circumstances beyond the original prohibition's reach. An expanded prohibition (issur mosif) also takes effect, because it adds an entirely new dimension of severity (such as forbidding benefit, not just consumption) that the first prohibition never covered. These two exceptions are the engine behind the extraordinary multi-offering cases explored on this daf.

slides.title: 🍽️ Building the Five Liabilities
slides.subtitle: Each new prohibition in the chain is inclusive or expanded — never a flat repeat
headers: Why the new prohibition takes effect
rows: Pure person eats chelev
Baseline: forbidden only due to the fat itself
He becomes impure
Inclusive — being impure adds prohibition even against pure pieces of the meat, so it lands atop the fat prohibition too
The animal is consecrated
Expanded — adds a benefit-prohibition beyond mere eating, so it also attaches to the chelev
It becomes leftover (notar)
Expanded — a prohibition against the altar itself is added, which then extends to the ordinary consumer too
It is eaten on Yom Kippur
Inclusive — the day's universal eating-ban extends even to consecrated leftover food

callout.label: Result:
callout.text: Five distinct legal 'reasons' stack on the very same bite — four sin offerings and one guilt offering (for misusing consecrated property), exactly as the previous daf's mishna described.

slides.title: ❓ Why Not Five, Six, or Even More?
slides.subtitle: The Gemara tests — and rejects — several ways to push the liability count higher

nodes.content: 🤔 Why not add piggul (improperly-intended offering) for a 5th sin offering?
🚫 Notar and piggul can never overlap on the very same olive-bulk — piggul, once it applies, blocks the meat from ever becoming notar
🤔 What about adding blood (dam) for a 6th sin offering?
🚫 The mishna describes one continuous act of swallowing — and the throat physically holds no more than two olive-bulks at once, capping how many prohibited foods can combine in a single act

✅ Two competing solutions instead reach 5 sin offerings validly: eating a kidney with its fat (reaching Yom Kippur's larger 'date-bulk' minimum), or eating an olive-bulk of piggul from a separate animal alongside the chelev

callout.label: Side note:
callout.text: A claim that Yom Kippur lacks the Shabbat-style prohibitions of 'joining courtyards' and carrying is raised (via Rafram) but ultimately rejected as a mistaken transmission (beruta).

slides.title: 👨‍👩‍👧 One Act, Six or Seven Sins
slides.subtitle: A series of mishnayot: forbidden relationships that compound through inclusive and expanded prohibitions
rows: Intercourse with one's daughter
Daughter, sister (if she was born of his mother), brother's wife, father's brother's wife, married woman, niddah
Intercourse with daughter's daughter
Granddaughter, daughter-in-law, brother's wife, father's brother's wife, wife's sister, married woman, niddah
Intercourse with wife's daughter
Same structure as the daughter case
Intercourse with wife's daughter's daughter
Same structure as the granddaughter case
Intercourse with mother-in-law
Mother-in-law, daughter-in-law, brother's wife, father's brother's wife, wife's sister, married woman, niddah

callout.label: How the categories accumulate:
callout.text: Each additional prohibition attaches only because the woman's status changes in a way that is inclusive or expanded relative to the man — e.g., she later marries his brother, or his father's brother, extending the forbidden scope without ever simply repeating an existing prohibition.

slides.title: ⚖️ Rabbi Yosei's Added Case
slides.subtitle: Reconciling his 'wife of father' addition with his stance elsewhere on competing prohibitions

lines.speaker: R' Yosei
lines.text: If the grandfather 'transgressed' and married the granddaughter, one is also liable for 'wife of his father' when engaging in relations with her.

lines.speaker: Challenge
lines.text: But how could the grandfather even marry her — she'd already be forbidden to him as his brother's former wife?

lines.speaker: R' Yoḥanan
lines.text: The marriage happened through levirate marriage (yibum), when the grandfather's brother died childless.

lines.speaker: Further challenge
lines.text: If it was valid yibum, why call it a 'transgression'? And separately — doesn't Rabbi Yosei elsewhere (Sanhedrin) hold that a later-arising prohibition does NOT create additional liability, sentencing only by the first prohibition to apply?

lines.speaker: Resolution
lines.text: Rabbi Ya'akov: he 'transgressed' a rabbinic secondary-relative restriction (his son's daughter-in-law). And Rabbi Abbahu/Rabbi Yoḥanan: Rabbi Yosei concedes specifically for an expanded prohibition — here, the added prohibition against another of the grandfather's own sons marrying her extends to him too.

callout.label: Consistent thread:
callout.text: Even a tanna who generally rejects layered liability still concedes the issur mosif exception — the same principle driving every multi-offering case on this daf.

summary.principle: A new prohibition takes legal effect atop an existing one only when it is 'inclusive' (extending scope to new people) or 'expanded' (adding a new dimension of severity) — never as a flat duplicate — and this single principle explains every case on the daf where one bite or one act of intercourse triggers multiple, distinct offerings.

flowSteps.content: 🔗 Rabbi Meir: a second prohibition takes effect only if inclusive or expanded, never a plain duplicate
🍽️ Five stacking prohibitions (chelev, impurity, hekdesh, notar, Yom Kippur) explain one bite's five offerings
❓ Attempts to push the count to six are rejected on physical/technical grounds (piggul-notar exclusivity, throat capacity)

columns.content: 👨‍👩‍👧 A series of mishnayot builds six- and seven-offering cases from compounding forbidden relationships
⚖️ Even Rabbi Yosei, who usually rejects layered liability, concedes the expanded-prohibition exception

flowSteps.content: 🎓 Key Principle: multiple liabilities from one act always trace back to genuinely new legal dimensions, not to repetition

quiz.q: According to Rabbi Meir, under what circumstances can a new prohibition take legal effect on something already forbidden by an earlier prohibition?
o: Never, under any circumstances
Only when the new prohibition is 'inclusive' (extending to new people/contexts) or 'expanded' (adding new severity)
Only on Yom Kippur
Always, without exception
quiz.e: Rabbi Meir holds that a prohibition generally cannot take effect where one already exists, except for an inclusive prohibition (issur kolel) or an expanded prohibition (issur mosif), both of which add a genuinely new legal dimension.

quiz.q: Why can't the prohibitions of notar and piggul both apply to the very same olive-bulk of meat, according to the Gemara?
o: Because notar and piggul are the same prohibition
Because once meat is rendered piggul, its piggul status prevents it from ever additionally becoming notar
Because piggul only applies to blood
Because notar cannot exist on Yom Kippur
quiz.e: The Gemara explains that piggul status, once it applies to a piece of meat, precludes that same piece from also becoming notar — the two statuses are mutually exclusive on the identical olive-bulk.

quiz.q: Why does the Gemara reject the possibility of a sixth sin offering (for blood) in the mishna's scenario of maximum liability from a single act of eating?
o: Because blood carries no punishment at all
Because the human throat physically cannot hold more than two olive-bulks at once during a single act of swallowing
Because blood is always kosher
Because Yom Kippur exempts blood consumption
quiz.e: The Gemara reasons that since the mishna describes a single continuous act of eating, and the throat holds no more than two olive-bulks at a time, there is a physical cap on how many distinct forbidden foods can combine within that one act.

quiz.q: According to the mishna, how many sin offerings can one be liable to bring for a single act of intercourse with one's daughter's daughter (granddaughter)?
o: Four
Five
Six
Seven
quiz.e: The mishna lists seven categories violated simultaneously: granddaughter, daughter-in-law, brother's wife, father's brother's wife, wife's sister, married woman, and niddah.

quiz.q: How do Rabbi Abbahu and Rabbi Yoḥanan reconcile Rabbi Yosei's ruling in this mishna (adding 'wife of father' liability) with his position elsewhere that a later prohibition does not create additional liability?
o: They say Rabbi Yosei retracted his other position entirely
They explain that Rabbi Yosei concedes specifically for an expanded prohibition (issur mosif), which is the case here
They say the two rulings are unrelated and cannot be reconciled
They say this mishna is not really attributed to Rabbi Yosei
quiz.e: Rabbi Abbahu and Rabbi Yoḥanan explain that even though Rabbi Yosei generally holds a later prohibition creates no additional liability, he concedes this is different for an expanded prohibition (issur mosif), which is what applies in this case.
